title: We shouldn't rush to judgment on police actions
article: There are rare occasions in which cops do use excessive violence or violate a suspect's Charter rights. And that is why there needs to be independent investigative bodies such as the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team or ASIRT. They insure cops aren't above the law.
But the first question critics should ask themselves before they condemn a cop involved in a shooting or use of a stun gun is: "What would I have done in the same situation?"
Monday, there was a fatality inquest into the shooting of Shawn Michael Price.
In the wee small hours of Sunday, May 10, 2009, a mugging victim flagged down a pair of Edmonton police officers. The victim gave police a description of two suspects.
Shortly after, the officers noticed a person matching one of the descriptions at the corner of 107 Ave. and 102 St., about block west of the downtown Brick furniture store.
When the two officers approached him, Shawn Michael Price, 36, was initially non-violent. But when they informed him he was being arrested, Price lunged for one of the officers' holstered pistols.

As Price and the 10-year veteran wrestled for his gun, the officer's partner first struck Price with her nightstick in a fruitless effort to convince him to surrender. Then she drew her own service pistol and shot Price in the hip in hopes of stopping him by wounding him.
When even that failed (and as she feared Price was getting closer to stealing her partner's gun), she shot Price through the chest and back at close range, killing him.
Price had a long history of crime and violence. At the time of his death, he was wanted on a Canada-wide warrant for leaving a halfway house.

He met his wife in the back of a prison van that was carrying both of them to jail. The pair honeymooned on a small island off Vancouver Island, but their marriage was cut short when Price was arrested at the Nanaimo ferry terminal on their return.

In 2007, Price confronted police with a knife after he had robbed a department store. That incident - less than two years before he was shot - ended with him slashing his own wrists and neck, then being charged with theft, resisting arrest and assault with a weapon.

On the night of his death, Price attempted for more than three minutes to snatch the veteran officer's gun. That may not sound like a long time, but in a life-and-death struggle, it must seem like an eternity.

It's also evidence the female officer who shot Price did not act in haste. She did not rush to judgment. She tried everything she could (neither she nor her partner had a Taser) to stop Price non-lethally. When those methods failed, what else was she supposed to do, let Price kill her partner? Kill her? An innocent bystander?
ASIRT also believe Price might have been high on cocaine at the time of his encounter with the cops.

At 2:00 in the morning, in a sketchy part of town, with a (possibly) drug-crazed career criminal trying to kill your partner, what would you do, especially considering that Price has been unfazed by several baton blows and even a slug to the hip?

Would you try to stay calm and hope Price eventually comes to his senses? Practise some deep-breathing exercises? Whip out a criminology textbook and consult the latest theories on non-violent conflict resolution? Or maybe you would suggest a comforting group hug, after which you promise to listen patiently to Price's story of his troubled childhood?
But more likely you would do exactly what the female officer did; shoot Price dead.
